title: Business and finance
subtitle: rise sharply, a fall of 5%, interest rate
summary: Describe how sales and prices go up and down, and use the language of profit, loans, interest and the economy.

lesson.heading: Rise and fall
lesson.text: These verbs describe **trends** (movements) in **sales** - how much you sell - and in prices. When sales or prices go up, we say they **rise**, **go up** or **increase**. When they go down, we say they **fall**, **go down** or **decrease**.

examples.note: gradually = slowly over a long period
sharply = quickly and by a large amount

examples.text: If prices do not rise or fall, they **stay the same**.

lesson.heading: Prepositions with rise and fall
lesson.text: We use certain prepositions to say by how much something rises or falls. **Rise**, **increase**, **fall** and **decrease** can also be nouns, each with its own preposition.

examples.text: There's been a gradual rise **in** prices.
We've seen a slight increase **in** profit.
Profits were £5 million, which is a decrease **of** 10%.

lesson.heading: profit or loss?

left.label: profit
left.text: The money you receive from your business after you have paid all your costs.
examples: Last year the company **made a profit** of £2 million.
We made a **profit** of six million euros.

right.label: loss
right.text: The opposite: the business pays out more than it receives.
examples: This year they could **make a loss**.
The company made a **loss** two years in a row.

lesson.note: In a row means one after another with no break.

rows: the system by which a country's trade, industry and money are organised

lesson.heading: Interest rates
lesson.text: **Interest** is what the bank **charges** you - asks you to pay - when you borrow money. The **interest rate** is how much you must pay as a percentage, e.g. 5% or 8%.

examples.text: If you borrow £100 for a year and the interest rate is 15% a year, you will **pay back** £115.
There are growing fears that **interest rates** could go up by as much as 2% next year.
Banks are reporting positive **signs** that the number of **loans** is increasing.
examples.note: a sign is something which shows that something is happening

lesson.heading: News in business English
lesson.text: Business news uses these words all the time. Note that **raise** is different from **rise**: you **raise** prices or hopes (you do it to something), but prices themselves **rise**.

examples.text: **Figures** published yesterday show that **trade** between the two countries has risen for the fifth year **in a row**.
The **value** of the pound fell slightly against the dollar.
The news has **raised** hopes that we may be coming out of **recession**.
The company decided to **raise** the price from £8.95 to £10.25.

lesson.text: Remember the pattern: prices rise *by* an amount, *from* one figure *to* another - and a rise or fall *of* 5% *in* sales.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: Sales rose ___ 10% last year.
exercises.explanation: We say prices or sales rise by an amount.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: The value of the shares fell ___ 240 pence to 225 pence.
exercises.explanation: We say something falls from one figure to another.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: There was a fall ___ 5% in the value of the shares.
exercises.explanation: The noun takes of before a percentage: a fall of 5%, a decrease of 10%.

exercises.prompt: There has been a gradual rise ___ profits.
exercises.explanation: A rise or an increase in something.

exercises.prompt: The company made a loss two years ___ a row.
exercises.explanation: In a row means one after another with no break.

exercises.prompt: The money a company receives for its goods after paying all its costs is called ___.
exercises.explanation: Profit is what is left after you have paid all your costs; the opposite is a loss.

exercises.prompt: You borrow £500 for a year and the bank ___ you 20% interest. You will pay back £600.
exercises.explanation: The bank charges you interest when you borrow money.

exercises.prompt: You take out a loan of £500 for one year and the interest rate is 15%. How much will you pay back?
exercises.explanation: 15% of £500 is £75, so you pay back £575.

exercises.prompt: Sales went up or down. Put each adverb or phrase in the right group.
Sales history: three years ago 100,000 units, two years ago 50,000 units. So sales did not fall slowly - there was a ___ fall in sales.
exercises.explanation: Sharp means quick and by a large amount.

exercises.prompt: Sales were 50,000 units two years ago and 50,000 units last year, so sales ___ the same.
exercises.explanation: If figures do not rise or fall, they stay the same.

exercises.prompt: In the first two ___ of this year, sales have risen from 50,000 to 80,000 units.
exercises.explanation: In business a quarter is a period of three months.

exercises.statement: The company decided to rise the price from £8.95 to £10.25.
exercises.explanation: The company decided to raise the price from £8.95 to £10.25. You raise prices, but prices rise.
